context: Current closing price of Chevron (CVX): $204.99 USD as of 2026-08-18.
justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I'll assume was a current price near $205, with each successive horizon incorporating a small positive expected return consistent with long-run equity risk premium assumptions. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of $205.5 essentially anchors near the last observed price, reflecting the well-documented near-random-walk behavior of equity prices over very short windows. The one-week estimate of $206 and one-month estimate of $207 embed a slight positive drift, consistent with annualized expected returns in the range of 7–10% for a broad equity index or similar instrument, scaled down proportionally to the forecast horizon. The incremental step-ups are deliberately small because mean reversion and drift effects are nearly imperceptible over days and weeks relative to the noise in returns.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, driven primarily by the square-root-of-time scaling of volatility. At one day, a ±$5 band around the estimate reflects daily volatility typical of a moderately volatile asset — roughly 2–2.5% implied daily move. By one week, the interval expands to ±$10, and at one month it reaches roughly ±$19, consistent with weekly and monthly volatility scaled from that daily figure. These widths also incorporate uncertainty about the volatility regime itself — whether realized volatility over the period will be calm or elevated — which adds a small amount of additional uncertainty beyond simple diffusion scaling.

Several specific risks could push outcomes well outside these stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden macroeconomic shock — such as an unexpected central bank policy shift, a geopolitical escalation, or a significant credit event — could produce gap moves far exceeding the lower bound of any of these intervals. A deterioration in liquidity conditions or a flash-crash dynamic could also compress prices rapidly. On the upside, a strong positive surprise in economic data, an unexpected dovish pivot from a major central bank, or a resolution of an ongoing geopolitical tension could drive sharp rallies that breach the upper bound. My stated 90% confidence intervals, by construction, are expected to be violated roughly 10% of the time, and fat-tailed return distributions in practice mean that when violations occur, they tend to be significantly outside the stated bounds rather than marginally so.
